title: PART I

nodes.title: Boeing Business and Operating Segments
nodes.summary: Boeing is a major aerospace company organized into three segments. Commercial Airplanes develops and markets passenger and cargo jets, including the 737, 767, 777 and 787, and continues developing the 777X and 737-7/-10. Defense, Space & Security develops and modifies military aircraft, weapons, rotorcraft, strategic defense and intelligence systems, cyber solutions, satellites and space-exploration products. Global Services supports commercial and defense customers with logistics, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, parts, training, documentation and digital services.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: The company owns numerous patents, licenses patents from others, and licenses its intellectual property to and from third parties. The U.S. government may use or authorize use of inventions developed under government contracts for government purposes. Unpatented research, development, engineering skills, trademarks, trade secrets, and other IP also support the business. Although IP collectively matters to all businesses, the company does not expect any single IP right’s expiration or patent-license termination to materially affect it.

nodes.title: Human Capital
nodes.summary: Boeing reports workforce growth from about 156,000 in 2022 to 171,000 in 2023, union representation and agreement expiration dates, and diversity data and inclusion initiatives, including employee resource groups. It describes competitive benefits, hiring and retention, employee feedback and recognition, skills and leadership development, learning and tuition programs, and commitments to workplace safety, quality, integrity, sustainability, ethical conduct, and channels for reporting concerns.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The commercial aircraft market faces intense global competition, including Airbus and Chinese entrants; the company is improving products, processes, and costs to compete on design, safety, quality, efficiency, and value. Defense faces major U.S. and international rivals, partnerships, and competitor teams, with competition expected to remain strong in 2024. Commercial and defense services are also highly competitive; BGS offers lifecycle services and aims to grow market share through customer satisfaction and productivity.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: The company operates in heavily regulated U.S. and international markets. Government contracts may be terminated for convenience or default, with different payment, recoupment, and damages consequences. Commercial aircraft must meet aviation safety and certification rules; the FAA is investigating the company’s quality system, increasing oversight, and blocking 737 MAX production increases or new lines until compliance is demonstrated. Environmental laws may raise costs and create material financial impacts, while the company monitors compliance. Non-U.S. sales face trade, investment, currency, political, economic, and other regulatory risks.

nodes.title: Raw Materials, Parts and Subassemblies
nodes.summary: The company depends on suppliers and subcontractors for essential materials, parts, and subassemblies. Key aerospace materials are aluminum, titanium, and carbon- or boron-based composites; although alternatives exist, qualifying sources may take a year or longer. The company stopped buying Russian titanium after the Russia-Ukraine war, with no operational disruption thanks to existing inventory and alternative sources. Many components and equipment items are sole-sourced, and the company works with those suppliers to maintain supply continuity.

nodes.title: Suppliers, Seasonality, Officers, and Company Information
nodes.summary: Boeing relies on U.S. and international suppliers and subcontractors, as well as affordable energy; failures may harm quality, schedules, and profitability. It monitors potential effects of the Israel–Gaza conflict on suppliers and customer operations. No material business seasonality is reported. Executive-officer information is referenced in Part III, Item 10. Boeing’s incorporation history, headquarters, and phone number are provided, along with its website and disclaimers; SEC filings are available there, and SEC registrant information is available at sec.gov.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
nodes.summary:
Item 1A. Risk Factors
An investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties, and our actual results and future trends may differ materially from our past or projected future performance. We urge investors to consider carefully the risk factors described below in evaluating the information contained in this report.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Business and Operations
We depend heavily on commercial airlines, subjecting us to unique risks.
key_items: Market conditions have a significant impact on demand for our commercial aircraft and related services

We enter into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which could subject us to losses if we have cost overruns or if increases in our costs exceed the applicable escalation rate
We derive a significant portion of our revenues from a limited number of commercial airlines
nodes.summary: The company’s reliance on commercial airlines exposes it to cyclical, competitive market risks. Aircraft demand and long-term backlog and deliveries depend on economic growth, political stability, airline profitability and financing, trade and international relations, technology, competition, fuel costs, security and health crises, and environmental rules. Economic, industry, or customer deterioration could reduce, delay, or cancel orders and payments, lowering revenue, profits, cash flow, and backlog over several years. Fixed-price contracts with indexed escalation create losses or margin pressure if costs rise faster than escalation, which fluctuates and is outside the company’s control. Revenue is concentrated among few airlines; customers may not exercise options or meet commitments, while fleet changes, consolidation, financial difficulties, rising costs, and inflation may further constrain sales and profits.

nodes.title: Our Commercial Airplanes business depends on our ability to maintain a healthy production system, ensure every airplane in our production system conforms to exacting specifications,
key_items: We must minimize disruption caused by production changes, achieve operational stability and implement productivity improvements in order to meet customer demand and maintain our profitabillty
If our commercial aircraft fail to satisfy performance and reliability requirements and/or potentially required sustainability standards, we could face additional costs and/or lower revenues
nodes.summary: Boeing’s commercial airplane business depends on safe, reliable production, supplier coordination, regulatory compliance, and successful aircraft development. Quality problems prompted an FAA investigation and increased oversight after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines accident; the FAA has halted 737 MAX production increases pending compliance, and Boeing cannot yet estimate the financial impact. Certification delays for the 777X and 737-7/-10, production disruptions, supply-chain and labor constraints, cost pressures, and performance or sustainability shortcomings could delay deliveries, trigger customer compensation or cancellations, increase costs, and reduce revenue and profitability.

nodes.title: Changes in levels of U.S. government defense spending or acquisition priorities, as well as significant delays in U.S. government appropriations, could negatively impact our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from unpredictable U.S. defense spending, delayed appropriations, shutdowns, and changing agency acquisition priorities, which could delay or reduce programs, disrupt operations, and harm financial results. Procurement shifts toward affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, and technical-data delivery may challenge the company and suppliers. Supplier financial, labor, quality, material, and single-source disruptions threaten deliveries and costs. Unionized workforces may strike or constrain operations, affecting production, customers, and revenue. Intense domestic and international competition, consolidation, budget pressure, and procurement rules may reduce contracts, sales, and cost competitiveness.

nodes.title: Supply Chain and Labor Risks
key_items: Our ability to deliver products and services that satisfy customer requirements is heavily dependent on the performance and financial stability of our subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of highly skilled labor, raw materials and other components.
Some of our and our suppliers’ workforces are represented by labor unions, which may lead to work stoppages.
nodes.summary: The company’s ability to meet customer requirements depends on supplier and subcontractor performance and financial stability, skilled labor, and access to materials and components. Inflation, resource and labor constraints, quality problems, financial difficulties, delays, high material costs, or disruptions to single-source suppliers may increase costs, delay deliveries, and harm financial results despite mitigation efforts. Union representation covers 33% of the workforce, and labor disputes, work stoppages, or limited workforce flexibility—including actions at suppliers—could delay production or development, strain customer relationships, and reduce revenue.

nodes.title: Competition within our markets and with respect to our products and services may reduce our future contracts and sales.
nodes.summary: Competition across Boeing’s markets may reduce future contracts and sales. Competitors may have stronger or more specialized capabilities. BCA faces aggressive international rivals; BDS expects intensified competition due to defense-industry consolidation, shifting acquisition and budget priorities, and customer cost pressures; and BGS faces many of the same strong competitors. International competition and cross-border consolidation are increasing, while U.S. procurement and compliance requirements may hinder cost competitiveness abroad. Boeing cannot assure successful competition, and these pressures could reduce revenue and market share.

nodes.title: We derive a significant portion of our revenues from non-U.S. sales and are subject to the risks of doing business in other countries.
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. customers, including foreign military sales, generated about 42% of 2023 revenue and are expected to remain significant. International business risks include regulatory and trade changes, government policies and local-content requirements, currency and political-economic volatility, sales intermediaries, customer financing and credit availability, taxes, export controls, tariffs, sanctions and embargoes, operational complexity, legal compliance, and unforeseen crises such as war or epidemics. U.S.-China tariffs affect some procured aircraft parts; Boeing uses duty-drawback procedures to mitigate costs. China is a key aircraft market and backlog contributor, so delivery disruptions or fewer orders could reduce deliveries and market share. Further geopolitical or trade deterioration could materially harm financial position, results, or cash flows.

nodes.title: We use estimates and make assumptions in accounting for contracts and programs. Changes in our estimates and/or assumptions could adversely affect our future financial results.
nodes.summary: The text explains that contract and program accounting relies on judgments and estimates of risks, revenues, costs, schedules, technical issues, incentives or penalties, claims, and award fees; changes can adversely affect future results. For commercial aircraft, program accounting allocates production, tooling, nonrecurring, and warranty costs across estimated program units, requiring assumptions about production volume and duration, prices, costs, and other factors. Orders, market studies, mix, rates, learning curves, escalation, suppliers, negotiations, claims, and certification risks—including for the 777X, 737-7, and 737-10—can change estimates. Different assumptions or circumstances may materially alter reported revenue and profit; further details are referenced in the company’s accounting-estimates discussion and financial-statement notes.

nodes.title: We may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/strategic alliances or divestitures.
nodes.summary: Mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, strategic alliances, and divestitures may fail to deliver expected benefits. Results depend on successful integration, portfolio and personnel performance, and partners; problems may cause legacy liabilities, transaction and intangible-amortization costs, asset impairments, guarantee or indemnity obligations, and changes from joint-venture consolidation. Despite risk-mitigation procedures, success is not assured. Divestitures may leave ongoing financial commitments, and former businesses’ nonperformance could trigger payments, higher costs, or write-downs.

This section covers risks from reliance on cyclical commercial-airline demand and concentrated customers; production quality, safety, certification, regulatory oversight, development, and delivery challenges; changing U.S. defense budgets and acquisition priorities; supplier, materials, and labor constraints; intense domestic and international competition; and international sales exposure to political, economic, trade, regulatory, currency, and geopolitical risks. It also addresses uncertainty in contract and program accounting estimates and the possibility that mergers, acquisitions, alliances, joint ventures, or divestitures will not deliver expected benefits. These factors may delay or cancel orders and deliveries, raise costs, reduce revenue, profits, cash flow, and market share, or otherwise harm financial results.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Contracts
key_items: We conduct a significant portion of our business pursuant to U.S. government contracts, which are subject to unique risks.
The U.S. government may modify, curtail or terminate one or more of our contracts
We are subject to U.S. government inquiries and investigations, including periodic audits of costs that we determine are reimbursable under U.S. government contracts
We enter into fixed-price contracts, which could subject us to losses if we have cost overruns.
We enter into cost-type contracts, which also carry risks.
We enter into contracts that include in-orbit incentive payments that subject us to risks.
nodes.summary: The company identifies risks from its substantial U.S. government contracting, including procurement-rule compliance costs, funding uncertainty, contract changes or termination, audits, repayment of disallowed costs, penalties, suspension or debarment, and reputational damage. Fixed-price contracts risk cost overruns, losses, and future charges or cash-flow impacts amid technical, supplier, production, quality, and labor problems; estimates and performance incentives are uncertain. Cost-type contracts risk reduced fees, profits, or cancellation. Satellite in-orbit incentives may be withheld or refunded if performance criteria are not met, potentially causing significant charges.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Cybersecurity and Business Disruptions
key_items: Unauthorized access to our, our customers’ and/or our suppliers’ information and systems could negatively impact our business.
Business disruptions could seriously affect our future sales and financial condition or increase our costs and expenses.
nodes.summary: The text describes cybersecurity risks from sophisticated, evolving attacks targeting Boeing, customers, suppliers, and third parties, potentially causing data or intellectual-property loss, operational disruption, compromised products, reputational damage, and regulatory or financial harm. Boeing uses security controls, monitoring, contracts, and oversight, but cannot guarantee prevention or timely response; past subsidiary incidents were not materially consequential, though future incidents could be. It also warns that physical threats, extreme weather and climate effects, natural disasters, pandemics, or other crises may disrupt Boeing or supplier operations, delay deliveries, increase costs, reduce sales, and damage reputation.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Matters
key_items: The outcome of litigation and of government inquiries and investigations involving our business is unpredictable, and an adverse decision in any such matter could have a material effect on our financial position and results of operations.
Our operations expose us to the risk of material environmental liabilities.
We may be adversely affected by global climate change or by legal, regulatory or market responses to such change.
nodes.summary: The text outlines legal, regulatory, environmental, and climate-related risks. Litigation and government inquiries or investigations may divert resources or lead to adverse rulings that materially affect financial results or cash flows. Environmental laws and liabilities—including cleanup, penalties, injury or property claims, acquired-company impacts, and indemnities—could generate added costs as rules, enforcement, or contamination findings change. Climate impacts and ESG expectations, regulations, contractual and policy demands, emissions standards, carbon pricing, disclosure, chemical restrictions, and water and waste requirements may raise costs, disrupt supply or production, constrain products, and harm competitiveness or reputation. Failure to meet or report publicly announced sustainability goals could also damage reputation or capital access.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity
key_items: We may be unable to obtain debt to fund our operations and contractual commitments at competitive rates, on commercially reasonable terms or in sufficient amounts.

Substantial pension and other postretirement benefit obligations have a material impact on our earnings, shareholders’ equity and cash flows from operations, and could have significant adverse impacts in future periods.
Our insurance coverage may be inadequate to cover all significant risk exposures.
A significant portion of our customer financing portfolio is concentrated among certain customers and in certain types of Boeing aircraft, which exposes us to concentration risks.
nodes.summary: The text outlines financing and liquidity risks from reliance on debt, $52.3 billion in debt, near-term repayments, and $17.0 billion in aircraft financing commitments, with market disruption, weaker performance, or credit downgrades potentially raising costs or limiting access. It describes pension and retiree health obligations whose funding, costs, equity, cash flow, and government-contract profitability depend on assumptions and markets. Insurance may not cover product-related liabilities, particularly outside U.S. SAFETY Act protections. Customer-financing concentration by customer, region, aircraft type, and credit quality risks losses if customers default, leases lapse, or aircraft values fall.

nodes.title: Risk Management and Strategy
nodes.summary: The company’s cybersecurity strategy focuses on threat detection, response, risk management, and resilience. Its risk-based safeguards use NIST and other standards and combine technical, physical, and administrative controls, policies, monitoring, training, oversight, audits, threat intelligence, partnerships, and third-party expertise. It monitors vulnerabilities and evaluates operational and financial impacts, integrating cyber risk into board-overseen enterprise and compliance risk programs. Preparedness includes technical and leadership tabletop exercises, annual employee training, monthly phishing simulations, and supplier risk oversight. Past incidents have not materially affected the company, but future incidents could; prevention and response processes cannot guarantee against material harm.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.summary: The Board oversees risk, with the Audit and Aerospace Safety Committees monitoring cybersecurity and reporting to the full Board. The Audit Committee reviews strategic, operational, and compliance risks; receives bimonthly CIO and CSO briefings; and has a cyber-expert member review strategy. Material events trigger notification and, if appropriate, committee or Board meetings. The Aerospace Safety Committee monitors threats to aerospace product safety through senior-management updates. The Board also receives annual CIO briefings. Management’s monthly Global Security Governance Council coordinates enterprise cybersecurity policy, strategy, prevention, detection, mitigation, and remediation, and tracks objectives with the Executive Council. Chaired by CSO Richard Puckett, an experienced security executive, it includes leaders across engineering, IT, safety, and product security. IT, security, audit, and legal teams coordinate timely issue response and required regulatory reporting.

nodes.title: Item 2. Properties
nodes.summary: As of December 31, 2023, the company had about 89 million square feet of productive space, approximately 86% in the United States, distributed among its businesses and classified as owned or leased. More than 82 million square feet were concentrated at listed major locations across the United States and several other countries. Airport runways and taxiways are generally used jointly under long-term government leases; the U.S. government also provides facilities and equipment for contract work. The company is involved in legal proceedings, with related contingencies discussed in Consolidated Financial Statement Note 21. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: The company is a global aerospace and defense leader that designs, manufactures, sells, services and supports commercial jetliners, military aircraft, satellites, missile defense, human spaceflight, launch systems and related services. It is one of two major manufacturers of 100-plus-seat commercial airplanes and a leading U.S. defense contractor, with U.S. operations and a growing international network of partners and suppliers. Its strategy focuses on three healthy core businesses: Commercial Airplanes, pursuing leadership through safe, high-quality, efficient, valuable airplanes and services; Defense, Space & Security, delivering affordable integrated solutions and pursuing next-generation programs and adjacent and international markets; and Global Services, providing innovative, comprehensive, cost-competitive commercial and defense support.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: Air travel largely recovered in 2023, with robust domestic and single-aisle demand, while international recovery—especially China’s—remains incomplete; airline demand and profitability are improving, though fuel, labor, economic, and geopolitical uncertainties persist. Supply-chain, quality, labor, and inflation pressures are hurting productivity, financial results, and cash flow. Long-term aviation prospects remain positive, with projected 3.5% fleet growth and demand for about 42,595 new airplanes over 20 years, but the industry faces external risks. BDS reports stable global defense demand but production disruptions, technical and supplier issues, and factory inefficiencies that have driven charges and weakened margins and cash flow. BGS expects strong commercial revenues and stable government-services demand.

nodes.summary: Revenue by segment for 2021–2023 totaled $62.286 billion, $66.608 billion, and $77.794 billion, respectively. 2023 growth of $11.186 billion reflected increases in Commercial Airplanes ($7.875 billion, chiefly higher 787 deliveries), Defense, Space & Security ($1.771 billion, mainly fixed-price development work), and Global Services ($1.516 billion, commercial services recovery). 2022 growth of $4.322 billion came from Commercial Airplanes (+$6.312 billion) and Global Services (+$1.283 billion), partly offset by Defense, Space & Security (−$3.378 billion) due to development-program charges, unfavorable performance, and lower P-8 and weapons volume. It details unallocated expenses (share-based compensation, deferred compensation, R&D, and eliminations), including market effects and the 737 MAX settlement, and summarizes pension costs and FAS/CAS adjustments.

nodes.title: Total Costs and Expenses (“Cost of Sales”)
nodes.summary: Cost of sales includes materials, labor, overhead and subcontracting; BCA mainly uses program accounting, long-term contract costs are recognized as incurred, and spare-parts costs use average cost. Cost of sales was $70.070 billion (90.1% of revenue) in 2023, $63.078 billion (94.7%) in 2022, and $59.237 billion (95.1%) in 2021. Increases reflected higher BCA/BGS revenue and, in 2022, BDS charges; the 2023 percentage decline reflected lower BDS development charges. R&D expense by segment totaled $3.377 billion in 2023, $2.852 billion in 2022, and $2.249 billion in 2021. Increases were driven mainly by 777X spending, plus 737 MAX and other BCA and enterprise product-development investments.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.summary: The text explains cost-of-sales accounting: long-term contract costs are recognized as incurred, most BDS and some BGS contracts span multiple years, and commercial spare-parts costs use average cost. Cost of sales was $70.070 billion in 2023 (90.1% of revenue), up $6.992 billion from 2022, mainly from higher BCA and BGS revenue, partly offset by lower BDS development charges; its revenue share fell due chiefly to lower BDS development charges. In 2022, cost of sales rose $3.841 billion to $63.078 billion, mainly from BDS charges and higher BCA revenue, while its revenue share was nearly unchanged. R&D expense by segment totaled $3.377 billion in 2023, $2.852 billion in 2022, and $2.249 billion in 2021. Increases reflected higher investment in 777X, 737 MAX, other BCA programs, and enterprise product development.

Contractual backlog excludes options, unexecuted announced orders, orders customers may unilaterally terminate, and unfunded government contracts; its 2023 increase was primarily due to higher BCA and BDS backlog. Delays to China deliveries or entry into service of the 777X, 737-7, or 737-10 could reduce backlog or cause significant cancellations. Unobligated backlog covers definitive government contracts without authorized funding and was largely unchanged.

nodes.summary: The text discusses risks from U.S. government funding deadlines, FY24–FY25 spending caps and potential sequestration; monitoring global trade, including U.S.–China tariffs and commercial relationships, steel and aluminum tariffs and agreements, and Russia-related sanctions and export controls; and supply-chain disruptions, labor instability, inflation, and possible effects of the Israel–Gaza conflict. nodes.summary: Boeing reports program updates: 737 accounting quantity and production rate, the Alaska Airlines door-plug accident, FAA grounding, inspections, quality-system investigation and oversight, production-rate restrictions, delayed 737-7/-10 certification due to de-icing changes, inventory and China deliveries, and potential financial impacts; earlier fuselage-hole rework is complete. The 747’s final delivery and immaterial closure impact are noted. The 767’s increased quantity, combined rate and near break-even commercial margins are described. For 777/777X, the text covers orders, rates, certification and delivery forecasts, resumed production, past abnormal costs and risks of future losses. For the 787, it covers orders, deliveries, rate increases, rework inventory and abnormal production costs. Fleet-support services and their expensing and historical cost share are summarized.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: Commercial aircraft development and production require complex supplier coordination, skilled labor, and costly, technically challenging efforts to meet customer and regulatory performance and reliability standards. New programs and derivatives face added schedule, production, certification, and global regulatory risks, threatening on-time delivery and profitability. Margins or program charges may be affected by accounting quantities, customer and model mix, costs and production rates, inflation-linked pricing, aircraft issues, capacity investment, learning, rework and safety changes, operational and supply-chain problems, cost reductions, regulatory demands, certification schedules, demand, and customer or supplier claims and negotiations. Technical complexity may increase completion costs or delay deliveries, potentially triggering cancellations, termination provisions, or other significant exposure, despite estimates considered appropriate.

nodes.title: United States Government Defense Environment Overview
nodes.summary: The FY24 U.S. budget request sought $842 billion for DoD and $27 billion for NASA, with no funding requested for F/A-18, V-22, or P-8 production aircraft; P-8 continues pursuing U.S. and international sales. Appropriation uncertainty and future budget cuts or shifting priorities could reduce, cancel, or delay programs and materially affect company results, financial position, or cash flows. Non-U.S. defense demand is driven by evolving security threats and modernization needs, creating opportunities across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East; non-U.S. customers accounted for 29% of BDS backlog at year-end 2023.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2023 operating results: revenue, share of company revenue, operating earnings or losses, and operating margins. It cautions that long-term contracts, varied delivery and milestone schedules, and differing order structures make period results and backlog comparisons unreliable indicators of future performance. It also lists annual deliveries by aircraft, helicopter, tanker, maritime-patrol, and satellite program, including new-build, remanufactured, and modified units, with totals of 169 in 2021, 165 in 2022, and 162 in 2023.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BDS revenues rose $1,771 million in 2023 versus 2022, a change not indicative of future trends. Revenue from five major fixed-price development programs increased $1,767 million, reflecting lower unfavorable cumulative catch-up adjustments and higher completion costs. Net unfavorable adjustments improved $648 million, mainly from lower development-program charges, partly offset by other-program performance. In 2022, revenues fell $3,378 million from 2021, chiefly due to development-program charges, other defense-program performance, and lower P-8 and weapons volume; catch-up adjustments were $1,858 million more unfavorable year over year.

nodes.title: (Loss)/earnings From Operations
nodes.summary: BDS operating losses narrowed to $1.764 billion in 2023 from $3.544 billion in 2022, mainly due to lower fixed-price development-program charges, partly offset by weaker results elsewhere and higher expenses. The text details losses and charges for key programs, contract catch-up adjustments, a $315 million satellite-customer impact, and equity-method income. It compares 2022 losses with 2021 earnings, explaining the deterioration and program charges. Backlog rose $4.639 billion to $59.012 billion. BDS development risks include cost-type and fixed-price contracts, technical and schedule issues, reach-forward losses, and potential future charges. BGS commercial-services volume exceeded pre-pandemic levels in 2023; revenues are expected to remain strong as aviation grows, with fleet expansion driving aftermarket demand and airlines increasingly using analytics and predictive maintenance.

nodes.title: BDS Backlog and Development Program Risks
nodes.summary: Reports 2022 fixed-price program charges and offsets, net cumulative contract catch-up losses, and BDS equity-method income for 2021–2023. BDS backlog was $59.012 billion at year-end 2023, up $4.639 billion year over year due to award and revenue timing. Development programs face cost, schedule, technical, and quality risks: cost-type contracts may yield reduced fees or cancellation; fixed-price programs may incur reach-forward losses, additional costs, delays, termination exposure, or future charges. The page also begins a Global Services section.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: BGS serves aerospace aftermarket, maintenance, training, logistics, and digital markets. Commercial services exceeded pre-pandemic levels in 2023 and are expected to grow as airlines use analytics, predictive maintenance, and outsourced spares management to improve efficiency. Government demand was stable; non-U.S. fleets are expected to grow faster than U.S. fleets, while military retirements will increase aging-aircraft and capability-upgrade needs. U.S. government spending uncertainty and intense global pricing competition pose risks. BGS revenue and operating earnings rose in 2023 and 2022, mainly on stronger commercial services; government performance, a discontinued engine distribution agreement, and contract catch-up adjustments also affected results. Revenue, company revenue share, earnings, and margins are reported for 2021–2023.

nodes.title: BGS Market Outlook and Operating Results
nodes.summary: The page describes demand for spare-parts efficiency and government services, including expected U.S. and international fleet trends, aircraft retirements, and risks from U.S. government spending limits. It notes intense aviation-services price competition and the importance of global market access. Results for 2021–2023 show revenue, share of company revenue, operating earnings, and margins. Revenue and earnings rose in both 2022 and 2023, mainly from commercial services recovery, higher volume, and favorable mix, with government-services weakness and contract catch-up adjustments also affecting comparisons.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: BGS backlog rose 3% to $19.9 billion at year-end 2023, mainly due to award timing. The text reviews 2021–2023 cash flows and drivers: operating cash improved in 2023 with higher revenue, advances and billings, partly offset by inventory growth; the 2022 improvement reflected working-capital changes, tax refunds and lower customer concessions, with comparisons to 2021. It notes supply-chain financing balances, investing cash flows and capital spending, financing outflows and debt repayments, year-end debt, employee tax-withholding share transfers, and suspended dividends.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: The text outlines contractual cash obligations as of December 2023 and liquidity resources: cash, short-term investments, operating cash flow, and $10 billion in revolving credit capacity, with facilities and maturities described. It reviews credit-rating outlook upgrades, risks to capital-market access and borrowing costs, and debt covenants, with compliance and substantial capacity. Pension obligations include GAAP underfunding, full ERISA funding, no expected significant 2024 contributions, possible higher future contributions, and stock funding for 401(k)s. It defines purchase obligations, details inventory and other commitments, customer support and escalation estimates, and $24.5 billion of industrial participation agreements through 2034, with no penalties in 2023. Off-balance-sheet arrangements, including guarantees, are referenced.

nodes.title: Commercial Commitments and Contingent Obligations
nodes.summary: Summarizes commercial commitments outstanding at December 31, 2023, including standby letters of credit, surety bonds, and aircraft financing commitments across funding periods. Customer financing commitments rose to $17.0 billion from $16.1 billion in 2022; the company expects third-party financing to reduce required funding but cannot guarantee it. Contingent obligations include pending legal proceedings, claims, and investigations, and environmental remediation, for which an $844 million liability was recorded.

nodes.title: Core Operating Earnings/(Loss), Core Operating Margin and Core Earnings/(Loss) Per Share
nodes.summary: The text explains Boeing’s non-GAAP core operating earnings, margin and earnings per share, their exclusions, and cautions that they supplement—not replace—GAAP measures and may differ across companies. It describes how GAAP and CAS pension costs are calculated and allocated, and how other postretirement costs are allocated. It reports 2021–2023 FAS/CAS service-cost adjustment and non-operating pension benefits, explains year-to-year changes, refers readers to related disclosures, and states management uses core measures to assess and forecast underlying performance because excluded benefit costs are largely market-driven or not allocable to U.S. government contracts.

nodes.title: Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Measures to GAAP Measures
nodes.summary: The text reconciles 2021–2023 non-GAAP core operating losses, margins and loss per share to GAAP results, including pension, postretirement and tax adjustments, weighted-average diluted shares, and definitions of adjustments. It then describes critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts: performance obligations, revenue and cost assumptions, quarterly reviews, cumulative catch-up and reach-forward losses, significant program losses in 2021–2023, risks and sensitivity to margin estimates. It begins outlining program accounting’s requirement to reliably estimate results across a defined production quantity.

nodes.title: Accounting for Long-term Contracts
nodes.summary: The text explains critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts, which are generally single performance obligations at BDS and some BGS operations. Revenue, costs, and profit are estimated using contract terms, costs incurred, and factors including options, incentives, inflation, technical and schedule risks, supplier performance, labor, and supply constraints. Estimates are reviewed quarterly; revisions may cause cumulative catch-up adjustments or immediate losses. Such adjustments increased operating losses by $2.943 billion in 2023, $5.253 billion in 2022, and $880 million in 2021, mainly on five fixed-price development programs, with further losses possible. Assumptions materially affect earnings; a 1% change in estimated margins on profitable contracts would alter 2023 pretax income by about $300 million. The text also introduces program accounting, which requires reliable estimates of revenues, costs, and margins across a defined production quantity.

nodes.title: Program Accounting
nodes.summary: The text explains critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts and commercial-aircraft program accounting. Long-term contract revenue, costs and profit require quarterly estimates and may generate cumulative catch-up adjustments or immediate loss charges; 2023–2021 adjustments increased operating losses, mainly on named fixed-price development programs, with future risk. Assumptions can materially affect earnings, including a roughly $300 million impact per 1% margin change. Program accounting estimates production quantities, prices and costs; new-aircraft development, certification and delivery pose risks. Margin changes are usually prospective, but anticipated program losses are charged immediately. The 767, 777X and 787 had near-break-even or single-digit margins, and a 1% commercial-program margin change could affect 2023 operating earnings by about $330 million.

nodes.title: Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Most employees in defined benefit plans have moved to a company-funded defined contribution plan. Annual pension measurements rely on assumptions, and changes or actual-versus-expected differences can materially affect expenses, obligations, and shareholders’ equity. A 25-basis-point discount-rate increase or decrease would reduce or raise the projected benefit obligation by $1.28 billion or $1.425 billion, respectively, with no significant pension-cost effect. A 25-basis-point change in expected asset returns would change 2023 pension cost by $150 million in the opposite direction. Note 16 provides three years of assumptions.

nodes.title: Deferred Income Taxes – Valuation Allowance
nodes.summary: The Company reported $14.743 billion in deferred tax assets and $10.363 billion in liabilities at year-end 2023. Quarterly, it assesses realizability using positive and negative evidence; recent losses preclude relying on projected earnings. Management estimates reversal timing, and a $4.550 billion valuation allowance—up $1.388 billion in 2023—mainly covers pension-related assets, losses, credits, and interest carryforwards; further allowances may affect earnings or comprehensive income. Market-risk disclosures describe fixed-rate debt exposure as immaterial; foreign-exchange and commodity hedges largely offset risks, with 10% price shifts changing unrealized losses by $361 million and $37 million, respectively. Deferred-compensation investments totaled a $1.6 billion liability; a 10% fair-value change would alter it by $164 million, recorded in operating earnings.

nodes.title: Market Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page discusses interest rate, foreign currency, and commodity price risks. Fixed-rate debt poses no material interest rate risk because investors generally cannot demand early repayment. Foreign currency forwards hedge committed and forecasted receipts and payments; a 10% exchange-rate change would shift unrealized losses by $361 million, offset by changes in hedged transactions, leaving no material combined risk. Commodity swaps and purchase contracts hedge production-related price changes; a 10% price change would shift derivative unrealized losses by $37 million, likewise offset by underlying transactions, with no material combined risk.

nodes.title: Market Risk
nodes.summary: Describes market risk from deferred compensation investments: at December 31, 2023, the mark-to-market liability was $1.6 billion, and a 10% fair-value change would alter it by $164 million, with liability changes recorded in operating earnings. Then provides the index to Item 8’s consolidated financial statements, segment data, Notes 1–23 covering accounting policies, financial accounts, taxes, compensation, equity, derivatives, fair value, legal matters, segments, and subsequent events, and independent auditor reports.

Presents Boeing’s 2021–2023 GAAP and non-GAAP financial results, revenues, costs, operating and net losses, margins, taxes, per-share results, segment performance, deliveries, and company, segment, and aircraft-program backlogs. Explains cost-of-sales, R&D, program and long-term contract accounting, development charges, program updates, market conditions, competition, government funding and defense demand, and operational, regulatory, supply-chain, and geopolitical risks. Also covers cash flows, liquidity, debt, pensions, commitments, contingencies, taxes, market risks, critical accounting estimates, non-GAAP reconciliations, and the financial-statement and auditor-report index.

summary: Part II reports Boeing’s NYSE listing, shareholder count, and 2023 share purchases, noting shares were withheld for employee taxes and none were repurchased on the open market. It introduces management’s discussion and analysis, company strategy and business segments, and commercial aviation, defense, and services market conditions and risks. It presents consolidated operating results and 2021–2023 GAAP and non-GAAP financial, segment, delivery, and backlog data, along with accounting policies, program developments, cash flow, liquidity, debt, pensions, commitments, contingencies, taxes, market risks, critical estimates, reconciliations, and financial-statement and auditor-report indexes.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Operations
key_items: Loss from operations; Loss before income taxes; Diluted loss per share
summary: Boeing’s consolidated statements of operations for 2021–2023 report product and service sales, total revenues, costs and expenses, operating-investment income, administrative and research expenses, disposition gains, operating losses, other income, interest and debt expense, pretax losses, income tax benefits or expenses, net losses attributable to noncontrolling interests and Boeing shareholders, and basic and diluted loss per share. Figures are in millions of dollars except per-share data; financial statement notes are referenced on pages 57–110.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
summary: A table of contents page presents Boeing’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income for 2023, 2022, and 2021, in millions of dollars. It reports net losses; other comprehensive income or loss, net of tax, from currency translation, investments, derivative instruments, defined-benefit pension and postretirement items, and equity-method investments; total other comprehensive results; comprehensive income or loss; amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests; and comprehensive income or loss attributable to Boeing shareholders. It refers readers to the financial statement notes on pages 57–110.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Financial Position
summary: Boeing’s consolidated statements of financial position compare 2023 and 2022, in millions of dollars except per-share data. They list assets (including cash, receivables, inventories, financing assets, property, goodwill, deferred taxes, investments, and other assets), liabilities (current and long-term), and shareholders’ equity or deficit, including stock, additional capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated comprehensive loss, and noncontrolling interests. Total assets and total liabilities and equity were $137,012 million in 2023 and $137,100 million in 2022. The statement refers readers to the notes on pages 57–110.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows
summary: A Boeing consolidated statement of cash flows for 2021–2023, in millions of dollars. It reports operating cash flows, reconciling net losses through noncash items and changes in assets and liabilities; investing cash flows from property, acquisitions, investments, and other activity; and financing cash flows from borrowings, repayments, stock options, taxes, and other items. It also shows exchange-rate effects, annual changes and opening and closing cash balances, restricted cash, and a reference to the financial-statement notes.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Equity
summary: A consolidated statement of equity for The Boeing Company and subsidiaries, in millions of dollars except per-share data, presents balances and changes for 2021–2023. It tracks common stock, additional paid-in capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, noncontrolling interests, and total equity. Changes include net losses, other comprehensive income or loss (net of specified taxes), share-based compensation, treasury shares issued for stock options, other share-based plans and 401(k) contributions, subsidiary shares purchased from noncontrolling interests, and other noncontrolling-interest changes. It refers readers to the financial statement notes on pages 57–110.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements Summary of Business Segment Data

nodes.title: Total revenues
nodes.summary: A table presents Boeing’s consolidated business segment financial data for 2021–2023, in millions of dollars. It lists revenues by Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and unallocated items, plus total revenue; operating losses by segment and related adjustments; other income, debt expense, pretax loss, income tax expense or benefit, net loss, noncontrolling interests, and net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders. It notes the data is integral to the financial statement notes and refers readers to Note 22 for further segment results.

nodes.title: Net loss
nodes.summary: The text presents Boeing’s 2021–2023 segment revenues, operating losses, other income and expenses, pretax results, taxes, net losses, and losses attributable to shareholders, directing readers to Note 22 for segment details. It then outlines accounting policies: consolidated entities and elimination of intercompany transactions; three reportable segments and reclassified prior periods; estimates under U.S. GAAP; contract-based operating cycles; and revenue recognition. Commercial aircraft revenue is recognized upon aircraft completion and customer acceptance, with program accounting for costs and contract payments treated as customary advances. Long-term defense and services contracts cover products and support across military, cybersecurity, space, and related activities.

nodes.title: Boeing Accounting Policies
key_items: Note 1 – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies Principles of Consolidation and Basis of Presentation
nodes.summary: Boeing’s consolidated financial statements cover the company and required consolidated subsidiaries and variable interest entities; significant intercompany balances and transactions are eliminated. Prior periods were reclassified to reflect its three reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, and Global Services. Preparing the statements under U.S. GAAP requires estimates and assumptions, so actual results may differ. For certain current assets and liabilities, Boeing uses the related contract or program duration as its operating cycle, generally longer than one year.

nodes.title: Revenue and Related Cost Recognition
nodes.summary: Describes revenue and cost recognition for commercial aircraft, long-term contracts, spare parts, services, concessions, contract assets/liabilities, financial services, and reinsurance. Covers transaction pricing, performance obligations, timing and measurement of revenue, payment terms, financing-component treatment, contract estimates and cumulative catch-up adjustments, reported losses and affected programs, and risks from changing estimates. Also explains lease and loan income, collectability, residual values and impairment; research and development expense and customer-funded arrangements; and share-based compensation measurement based on grant-date fair value.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.summary: The text describes policies for assessing financing-receivable collectability and past-due status, suspending income and handling revenue and interest for non-accrual customers. It explains how lease residual values are estimated and impairments recognized; operating-lease revenue, depreciation, held-for-sale valuation, and impairment accounting; and workers’ compensation reinsurance participation, revenue and cost amounts for 2021–2023, and net presentation. It also covers research and development cost recognition, customer-funded best-efforts arrangements, and bid-and-proposal expenses for 2021–2023.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: Share-based compensation for share-settled awards uses grant-date fair value, while cash-settled or cash-settleable awards use reporting-date fair value; both are net of estimated forfeitures and expensed over the service/vesting period. Income taxes reflect current law, timing differences, rate changes, uncertain tax positions under a more-likely-than-not threshold, related interest and penalties, and valuation allowances for deferred tax assets unlikely to be realized. Pension and other postretirement benefits are calculated using actuarial methods and assumptions, with gains and losses recorded in equity and, above a threshold, amortized; plan funded status is reported on the balance sheet. Postemployment benefit liabilities are recorded when payment is probable, estimable, and tied to vested or accumulated rights.

nodes.title: Income Taxes and Employee Benefit Plans
nodes.summary: Explains income tax calculation, uncertain tax positions, tax interest and penalties, and valuation allowances for deferred tax assets. Describes pension and other postretirement benefits, including plan transitions, benefit calculation, actuarial assumptions and gains or losses, and balance-sheet recognition of funded status. States that postemployment benefit liabilities are recorded when payment is probable, estimable, and tied to vested or accumulated rights.

nodes.title: Environmental Remediation and Cash Accounting
nodes.summary: The company assesses environmental remediation obligations and recoveries through studies, expert analyses, and legal reviews. It accrues probable, estimable liabilities at its best estimate or the low end of a reasonable range; costs are not discounted, and recoveries are recorded when probable. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with original maturities of three months or less. Eligible bank balances are aggregated, and negative balances, mainly uncleared checks, are reclassified to accounts payable; these totaled $117 million and $102 million at December 31, 2023 and 2022, respectively.

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.summary: Inventories for aircraft programs and long-term contracts include direct and overhead costs, subject to net realizable value limits; abnormal or inapplicable fixed costs are expensed, and some costs extend beyond one year. Government-contract inventory includes allowable manufacturing-reengineering costs. Commercial program inventory includes deferred early-production costs, expected to be recovered over program deliveries, and supplier advances, transferred to work in process as parts arrive. Quarterly reviews assess completion costs and revenues, recording contract or program loss provisions when costs exceed revenue. Used aircraft and general materials are carried at cost up to net realizable value; spare parts at the lower of average cost or net realizable value. Quarterly impairment reviews consider sales, production needs, and fleet characteristics; impairments are expensed. Airline early issue sales consideration is recorded in inventory and reduces revenue upon aircraft delivery; unrecoverable amounts are written off.

nodes.title: Precontract Costs
nodes.summary: Precontract costs deemed recoverable from future orders are capitalized in inventory, except start-up costs, which are expensed; capitalized amounts are written off if recovery becomes unlikely. Property and equipment are recorded at cost, including construction-period interest, and depreciated using specified useful lives and methods; internal-use and hosted software costs are capitalized in other assets and amortized over five years or the hosting term. Useful lives are reviewed, and assets held for sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair value less selling costs. Held-for-use assets are tested for impairment when indicated, with losses based on carrying value versus fair value if undiscounted cash flows cannot recover it. Lease classification is assessed at inception; operating and finance lease assets and liabilities are presented in specified balance-sheet accounts. Operating lease assets and liabilities are recognized at commencement using the present value of lease payments and an estimated incremental borrowing rate.

nodes.title: Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for inventory, including valuation, quarterly impairment reviews, expense recognition, and treatment of airline early issue sales consideration; capitalization and potential write-off of recoverable precontract costs; property, plant, and equipment costs, depreciation lives and methods, software amortization, and periodic life reviews; and impairment rules for long-lived assets held for sale or use. It also describes lease identification, balance-sheet classification, measurement of operating lease assets and liabilities, payment exclusions, term options, straight-line expense, and combining real-property lease and non-lease components.

nodes.title: Asset Retirement Obligations
nodes.summary: The company records known asset retirement obligations when fair value is reasonably estimable, including certain asbestos removal, decommissioning, and lease restoration costs; recorded amounts are immaterial. Known conditional obligations are unrecorded when settlement timing or method is too uncertain, and will be recognized once estimable. Potential undiscovered obligations, such as unknown asbestos, are also excluded from the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually and when impairment indicators arise; the text outlines qualitative and quantitative goodwill tests, IPR&D accounting and impairment, and useful lives and impairment tests for finite-lived intangibles. It describes accounting for time deposits, available-for-sale debt and equity-method and other equity investments, including impairment reviews and operating versus non-operating income classification. Derivatives are measured at fair value; cash-flow hedge changes are deferred and reclassified to earnings, while undesignated derivative changes enter earnings immediately. Allowances for credit losses on specified financial assets are assessed quarterly using credit-related factors.

nodes.title: Investment and Derivative Accounting
nodes.summary: The page explains investment accounting: time deposits are carried at cost; available-for-sale debt securities are measured at fair value, with unrealized gains and losses in other comprehensive income, realized results based on specific identification, and quarterly impairment assessments. It describes equity-method and other equity investment measurement, impairment, and cash-flow treatment, and classifies investment earnings as operating or non-operating. All derivatives are measured at fair value; cash-flow hedge results are initially recorded in comprehensive income and later reclassified to earnings. Aluminum purchase and sale agreements and other non-designated derivatives have fair-value changes recognized immediately in earnings.

nodes.title: Allowances for Losses on Certain Financial Assets
nodes.summary: The company establishes and quarterly evaluates credit-loss allowances for receivables and other financial assets using customer credit ratings, bankruptcy information, default and expected loss rates, receivable age, and collateral exposure. Customer ratings rely on public and directly obtained information and align with major agency categories. Financing receivables are secured by related assets; aircraft collateral values generally use median estimates from multiple third-party publications, with judgment for atypical aircraft or equipment. Some customer agreements also allow recovery from other customer assets if collateral sale proceeds fall short of the receivable balance.

nodes.title: Commercial Aircraft Trade-in Commitments
nodes.summary: The company’s sale agreements for new commercial aircraft may grant customers the right to trade in used aircraft at specified prices. Exposure is recorded as a revenue adjustment at delivery for the difference between the agreed trade-in price and estimated fair value, and/or as a cost-of-products charge for subsequent adverse value changes before purchase; current estimates are accrued as liabilities. Valuations use aircraft-specific characteristics, market conditions, and multiple sources, considering resale (including storage), leasing (including refurbishment), or scrap markets. Analyses are updated quarterly using placement activity or published third-party values adjusted for aircraft attributes and known conditions.

nodes.title: Warranties
nodes.summary: The text describes product warranties, mainly issued by the BCA segment for commercial aircraft (typically 3–4 years) and by BDS for military aircraft and weapons (typically six months to two years). Standard costs are accrued upon delivery; liabilities reflect remaining coverage, historical claims, and major issues, including fleet-wide corrective commitments. Aircraft performance guarantees are treated as warranties, with estimated payments reducing revenue at delivery; supplier recovery claims reduce product costs and are included in program estimates. Supplier penalties are accrued when probable and estimable. Guarantees are initially recorded at fair value, with credit-guarantee losses based on default probability, exposure, and expected recovery; contingent-loss liabilities are updated quarterly.

nodes.title: Warranties, Supplier Penalties, and Guarantees
nodes.summary: The page describes warranties for commercial and military products, their coverage periods, and how standard and major-issue costs are estimated and recorded. Aircraft performance guarantees are treated as warranties, with estimated payments reducing revenue at delivery; supplier recoveries are recorded as inventory and reductions in product costs, and both are included in program completion estimates. Supplier penalties are accrued when probable and estimable. Guarantee liabilities are recorded at inception at fair value; credit-guarantee expected losses reflect default probability and recoveries, with contingent-loss liabilities adjusted quarterly.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: Note 2 reports goodwill balances by business segment and changes through December 31, 2023, including acquisitions and adjustments, with total goodwill of $8.093 billion. It gives carrying amounts for indefinite-lived trade names ($197 million) and in-process research and development ($202 million) in 2023 and 2022, and gross amounts and accumulated amortization for finite-lived acquired intangibles by category. Amortization expense was $235 million in 2023 and $241 million in 2022; estimated annual expense for 2024–2028 ranges from $224 million to $147 million.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: Boeing calculates basic and diluted EPS using the two-class method, allocating undistributed earnings equally between common shares and participating securities; diluted shares use the treasury stock method. For 2023, 2022, and 2021, net losses attributable and available to common shareholders were $2.222 billion, $4.935 billion, and $4.202 billion, respectively; basic and diluted weighted-average common shares were 605.8 million, 594.9 million, and 587.6 million, yielding basic and diluted losses per share of $3.67, $8.30, and $7.15. Participating securities include certain deferred-compensation instruments. Antidilutive potential shares excluded due to strike prices or unmet performance conditions comprised performance awards, performance-based restricted stock units, restricted stock units, and options; further exclusions of 5.7 million, 3.5 million, and 2.6 million shares in 2023, 2022, and 2021 resulted from net losses.

nodes.title: Note 4 – Income Taxes
nodes.summary: Notes 4–6 cover income taxes, receivables, and credit-loss allowances. They report pretax losses, current and deferred tax expense or benefits, tax-rate reconciliations, deferred-tax assets and liabilities, carryforward expirations, and valuation allowances. The text explains loss-related limits on deferred-tax-asset realization, 2023 allowance changes, indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings, tax interest and penalties, unrecognized tax benefits, audits, possible audit adjustments, and expected Pillar Two effects. It also details accounts receivable by category and annual changes in allowances for expected credit losses across receivable and other asset types.

nodes.title: Tax Uncertainties, Receivables, and Credit Loss Allowances
key_items: Note 6 – Allowances for Losses on Financial Assets
nodes.summary: Describes uncertainty in audit settlements and potential decreases in unrecognized tax benefits, plus the expected limited effect of OECD Pillar Two’s 15% global minimum tax. Reports 2023 and 2022 net accounts receivable by customer category, including valuation allowances and related footnotes. Reconciles expected-credit-loss allowances for accounts receivable, unbilled receivables, other current assets, financing receivables, and other assets for 2022 and 2023.

nodes.title: Inventories and Commercial Aircraft Programs
nodes.summary: Inventories totaled $79.741 billion in 2023 versus $78.151 billion in 2022, comprising aircraft programs, long-term contracts, capitalized precontract costs, spare parts and other items; precontract costs included KC-46A, Commercial Crew and T-7A options. The note details 737, 777X and 787 inventory costs and expected recoveries from firm and future orders. It reports 777X production pauses, resumption and abnormal costs, and 787 low-rate production and abnormal costs expensed in 2021–2023, with remaining rework costs expected to be insignificant. Early issue sales consideration to airline customers was $4.126 billion in 2023 and $3.586 billion in 2022.

nodes.title: Note 8 – Contracts with Customers
nodes.summary: Unbilled receivables fell from $8,634 in 2022 to $8,317 in 2023, mainly due to increased billings at BDS and BGS. The table reports long-term contract assets that were unbillable or related to outstanding claims, including current and post-one-year amounts and valuation allowances. Commercial-incentive unbilled receivables collectible after one year were $42 in 2023 and $117 in 2022; claims are believed earned but remain uncertain in determination or realization. Advances and progress billings rose from $53,081 to $56,328, driven mainly by BCA order advances, partly offset by BDS revenue recognition. Revenue recognized from beginning-of-year balances was $15,298 in 2023 and $12,087 in 2022.

nodes.title: Note 9 – Financing Receivables and Operating Lease Equipment
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2023, net financing receivables were $1.134 billion and operating lease equipment was $470 million, for combined assets of $959 million, compared with $1.604 billion in 2022. Financing arrangements run 1–12 years and may include extensions, termination, or aircraft purchase options. Receivables of $44 million in 2023 and $405 million in 2022 were uncollectible and on non-accrual; the allowance was largely unchanged. Sales-type lease investment comprised gross payments, unearned income, net payments, and residual assets. Financing interest income was $108 million in 2023 and $13 million in 2022; $9 million was past due in 2023. The text also presents 2023 receivables by credit rating and origination year and allowance default rates for CCC, B, BB, and BBB exposures of 100.0%, 0.0%, 2.4%, and 0.1%, respectively.

nodes.title: Financing Receivables Exposure
nodes.summary: The text details financing receivables and operating-lease equipment concentrated in specified Boeing aircraft models, with 2023 and 2022 balances and identification of operating versus sales-type leases. Operating-lease assets are primarily commercial jets; impairment charges were $0, $7, and $31 million in 2023–2021. Lease income included sales-type interest of $55, $69, and $54 million and operating payments of $60, $65, and $68 million; commencement profit on sales-type leases was $32, $28, and $78 million. It also presents 2023 undiscounted receipts by year and category, imputed interest, residual values, and unguaranteed residual values of $21 million in 2023 versus $86 million in 2022.

nodes.title: Note 10 – Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 10 reports property, plant and equipment balances at December 31, 2023 and 2022: gross assets by category (land, buildings and improvements, machinery and equipment, and construction in progress), accumulated depreciation, and net totals. It also gives depreciation expense and capitalized interest for 2021–2023, non-cash PP&E acquisitions for 2022–2023, and accounts payable for PP&E purchases at each year-end.

nodes.title: Investments and Equity Method Holdings
nodes.summary: Note 11 reports investments of $4.309 billion at December 31, 2023, versus $3.589 billion in 2022, including time deposits, equity-method holdings, available-for-sale debt, equity and other investments, and restricted cash. It explains classifications, dividends and undistributed equity-method earnings, restricted-cash purposes, investment-related cash flows and time-deposit purchases and maturities. Available-for-sale debt investments are assessed quarterly; all were investment grade, with no credit-loss allowance. Equity-method holdings totaled $966 million in 2023 and $948 million in 2022, including United Launch Alliance and other investments, with ownership and segment information.

nodes.title: Note 12 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 12 reports operating lease expenses for 2023 and 2022, including variable expenses, cash payments and noncash additions. It details year-end right-of-use assets and current and noncurrent liabilities, remaining lease terms, discount rates, balance-sheet classifications, and lease-payment maturities through 2028 and thereafter. It also notes $430 of leases not yet commenced, mainly for a military aircraft maintenance hangar, starting in 2024 with 2–27-year terms. Note 13 lists accrued-liability categories and totals for 2023 and 2022.

nodes.title: 737 MAX Customer Concessions and Other Considerations
nodes.summary: The table shows 737 MAX customer concessions and other considerations liability movements for 2023 and 2022: balances began at $1.864 billion and $2.940 billion, respectively, and ended at $1.327 billion and $1.864 billion after reductions for payments, concessions and in-kind considerations, and estimate changes. At year-end 2023, $0.1 billion remained under customer negotiation; $0.6 billion is expected to be paid in 2024, with the rest settled through lower customer delivery payments.

nodes.title: Environmental
nodes.summary: Environmental remediation liabilities rose from $752 million in 2022 to $844 million in 2023, reflecting payments net of recoveries and estimate changes. Recorded amounts represent best estimates or the low end of reasonably possible costs, including up to 30 years of site maintenance; actual costs may be higher, some obligations cannot be estimated, and the high-end estimate exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,058 million in 2022 and $1,030 million in 2023. Product warranty liabilities increased from $2,275 million to $2,448 million after additions, payments, and estimate changes. Aircraft trade-in commitments allow certain customers to exchange used aircraft at specified prices; exercise likelihood is assessed periodically, and agreements have notice, timing, and mutual-termination provisions. Commitments expire from 2024–2030; total contractual amounts were $1,117 million in 2022 and $1,415 million in 2023, with probable net payments and related aircraft fair values of $286 million and $407 million, respectively.

nodes.title: Remediation Estimates, Warranties, and Aircraft Trade-Ins
nodes.summary: The page notes that high-end reasonably possible remediation costs exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,030 in 2023 and $1,058 in 2022, while some obligations cannot be estimated. A warranty-liability table shows beginning balances, additions, payments, estimate changes, and ending balances for 2023 and 2022. It describes aircraft trade-in commitments, how exercise likelihood is assessed, and their terms. Commitments expired between 2024 and 2030; contractual totals were $1,415 and $1,117, with probable net payments and related aircraft fair values of $407 and $286, respectively, at year-end 2023 and 2022.

nodes.title: Financial Commitments and Financing Programs
key_items: Standby Letters of Credit and Surety Bonds
nodes.summary: The page details aircraft financing commitments of $17.0 billion at year-end 2023, their expected funding schedule, below-investment-grade customer credit, and the conclusion that no loss reserve is needed; $264 million of future joint-venture contributions; standby letters of credit and surety bonds of $4.548 billion; legacy COLI obligations, policy values, loans, and net presentation; and supplier financing programs, including $2.9 billion in 2023 payables, payment terms, and the view that changes in program availability would not significantly affect liquidity.

nodes.title: Government Assistance and Contract Risks
nodes.summary: The page describes state, local, and Australian grants and tax incentives, their recorded benefits, balances, eligibility conditions, and potential clawbacks, as well as Missouri industrial revenue bond financing and related tax abatements. It explains that U.S. government contract costs are audited and disputed costs may require reserves, earnings charges, or refunds. Fixed-price development contracts carry uncertain cost and timing risks that may lead to losses, charges, termination, cancellations, or other significant exposure.

nodes.title: VC-25B Presidential Aircraft
nodes.summary: The text reports loss increases and remaining risk across Boeing’s fixed-price defense and space programs. VC-25B development of two aircraft saw 2023 losses rise $482 due to engineering changes, supplier negotiations, and factory labor instability. KC-46A’s 2023 loss rose $309 from factory disruption and supplier-quality rework; ten production lots covering 139 aircraft were authorized, with future-lot costs and liabilities disclosed. MQ-25’s loss rose $231 amid production and flight-test delays and higher costs. T-7A’s loss rose $275 due to higher estimated production costs, with future-lot costs and liabilities disclosed. Commercial Crew’s Starliner loss rose $288 in 2023 after a crewed-flight-test delay; its uncrewed orbital test succeeded in 2022.

nodes.title: Military Aircraft Program Contracts and Losses
key_items: T-7A Red Hawk EMD Contract & Production Options
nodes.summary: The page reviews contract scope, production options, progress, and estimated losses for the KC-46A tanker, MQ-25, and T-7A Red Hawk programs. It describes contract awards and aircraft quantities, 2022–2023 increases in reach-forward losses and their causes, and related precontract costs or supplier termination liabilities. Each program retains a risk of additional future losses.

nodes.title: Commercial Crew
nodes.summary: NASA contracted the company to design and build the CST-100 Starliner to carry crews to the International Space Station. The uncrewed Orbital Flight Test was completed in the second quarter of 2022. Reach-forward losses increased by $288 in both 2022 and 2023; the 2023 increase was primarily due to delaying the crewed flight test after a parachute supplier identified a testing issue. The test is planned for April 2024. At year-end 2023, the company had approximately $226 in capitalized precontract costs and $160 in potential supplier termination liabilities for unauthorized future missions, with risk of further losses.

nodes.title: Note 14 – Arrangements with Off-Balance Sheet Risk
nodes.summary: The note describes off-balance-sheet risks, mainly third-party guarantees. It reports maximum potential guarantee payments of $404 million in 2023 versus $514 million in 2022, estimated collateral/recourse proceeds, and liabilities recorded in accrued liabilities. Aircraft repurchase commitments generally apply 10–15 years after delivery, depend on a future aircraft-sale agreement, and rarely become trade-ins; expected proceeds reflect the lower of contracted price or estimated fair value. Credit guarantees cover lessee or debtor defaults and expire through 2036. Indefinite environmental and other indemnities related to business and facility sales cannot be quantified; estimable or probable claims are included in Note 13 environmental liabilities.

nodes.title: Debt, Credit Facilities and Repayment Schedule
nodes.summary: Note 15 describes revolving credit agreements, their maturities and term-out option, $10 billion of available credit at year-end 2023, and covenant compliance. It reports interest incurred and paid for 2021–2023, current debt balances for 2022–2023, and total debt by unsecured interest-rate/maturity bands, finance leases, and other notes. It also presents scheduled debt principal payments and minimum finance lease obligations for 2024–2028.

nodes.title: Note 16 – Postretirement Plans
nodes.summary: Note 16 describes postretirement plans: most employees with defined-benefit pensions have moved to company-funded defined-contribution plans; major pension plans are trust-funded to meet current and future obligations. Other postretirement benefits are mainly retiree health care, generally until age 65, with lifetime coverage for certain groups, plus limited life insurance. Funded status is fair-value plan assets minus projected benefit obligations; overfunded and underfunded balances and amounts payable within 12 months are classified in specified asset and liability accounts. Tables report pension and other postretirement benefit costs/income for 2021–2023, including their operating and nonoperating components, and introduce tables of 2022–2023 changes in obligations, assets, and funded status.
