nodes.title: Assumptions
nodes.summary: The text presents weighted-average assumptions used to measure benefit obligations at year-end and calculate the following year’s net periodic benefit cost. For 2021–2023 it lists pension and other postretirement discount rates, expected asset returns, compensation growth, and cash-balance interest-crediting rates. It explains that discount rates come from a high-quality bond yield curve, excluding the highest and lowest 10% of yields, and are applied to projected benefit payments. Expected asset returns reflect historical experience and prospective asset-class performance; costs use a five-year moving-average market-related asset value, which exceeded fair value by about $8.466 million in 2023. It also gives health-care cost trend assumptions, including next-year and ultimate rates and the year the ultimate rate is reached.

nodes.title: Plan Assets
nodes.summary: Describes pension asset objectives, strategic allocation and 2023 allocation review, target and actual asset-class percentages for 2022–23, investment types, manager and derivative use, and liquidation of company stock. Outlines risk controls and fair-value hierarchy, asset values by level for 2022–23, valuation methods and inputs by investment type, and Level 3 asset rollforwards and unrealized results. Also notes OPB assets’ balanced index-fund composition, Level 1 valuation, and immaterial effect of expected returns on benefit cost.

nodes.title: Pension Cash Flows and Compensation Plans
nodes.summary: Required pension contributions, including non-U.S. funding, are not expected to be significant in 2024, and no discretionary contributions are planned. Estimated pension and other postretirement benefit payments are listed for 2024–2033, including gross benefits, subsidies, and net benefits. Certain plans specify how assets are allocated after an unapproved change in control and termination, and allow the U.S. government a fair share of surplus assets linked to reimbursed contract contributions. Eligible employees may participate in defined contribution plans, principally 401(k)s; expenses were $1,564 million in 2023, $1,260 million in 2022, and $1,268 million in 2021.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: The 2023 Incentive Stock Plan authorizes 12.9 million shares plus certain shares remaining from the superseded 2003 plan and permits various equity and cash awards to employees and other eligible recipients. Awards are funded with treasury shares, with new shares used if needed; treasury shares are expected to suffice in 2024. Share-based compensation expense and related tax benefits are reported for 2021–2023 and allocated across expenses and inventory. The text describes option vesting, expiration, retirement-related treatment, valuation methodology and assumptions, and 2021–2022 executive option grants, including premium exercise prices and performance-based reductions. Earlier options vested over three years and were fully vested by 2017.

nodes.title: Stock Options
nodes.summary: Share-based compensation expense, primarily in total costs, general and administrative expenses, and inventoried production costs, was $697, $726, and $840 in 2023, 2022, and 2021; related income tax benefits were $157, $178, and $148. Executive stock options generally vest after three years and expire after ten, with special provisions for qualifying terminations; valuations use Monte Carlo simulations without expected dividends. No material options were granted in 2023. The text describes 2022 and 2021 premium-priced and other grants, valuation assumptions, and older options’ vesting. In 2023, options outstanding fell to 792,662 after grants, exercises, and forfeitures; 7,953 were exercisable. It reports weighted-average exercise prices, remaining life and intrinsic value, exercise intrinsic values and tax benefits for 2021–2023, and $11 of unrecognized option compensation cost expected to be recognized over 1.2 years.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text describes Boeing’s 2021–2023 executive RSU grants, including accelerated 2022 awards, vesting and termination rules, grant-date valuation, and 2023 RSU activity, costs, and amortization periods by award category. It also covers 2023 executive PRSUs tied to 2023–2025 cumulative free cash flow, their payout and vesting terms, and compensation cost; PBRSUs tied to peer-relative total shareholder return, which expired in 2023 with no payout; the employee stock purchase plan’s discount, share authorization, and 2023 purchases; and deferred compensation plans allowing eligible staff to defer pay, incentives, and retirement contributions.

nodes.title: Equity Awards and Employee Stock Purchase Plan
nodes.summary: Reports 2023 RSU activity, including beginning, granted, forfeited, distributed, and ending units, vested units, and unrecognized compensation costs and amortization periods. Describes executive PRSUs granted in 2023, their performance-based 0%–200% payout, vesting, settlement, termination eligibility, and year-end compensation data. PBRSUs pay according to three-year relative TSR and expired in 2023 with no payout. The employee stock purchase plan offers eligible employees shares at 95% of period-end fair market value; 12 million shares are authorized, and about 216,719 were purchased in 2023 at an average $193.52 per share.

nodes.title: Deferred Compensation
nodes.summary: The Company’s deferred compensation plans allow certain employees and executives to defer salary, bonuses, other incentive awards and retirement contributions, allocating them among 23 investment funds, including a Boeing stock unit account. Related expense/(income) was $188 million in 2023, $(117) million in 2022 and $126 million in 2021; marked-to-market liabilities were $1,640 million and $1,499 million at year-end 2023 and 2022. Shareholders’ equity disclosures state that 1.2 billion common and 20 million preferred shares were authorized, with no preferred shares issued, and provide 2021–2023 common and treasury share balances and activity. Additional paid-in capital decreased $267 million in 2023 due to a noncash purchase of shares in a consolidated subsidiary from noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: Shareholders’ Equity and Deferred Compensation
nodes.summary: Participants may allocate deferred compensation among 23 investment funds, including a Boeing stock unit account. Related expense/(income) was $188, ($117), and $126 in 2023, 2022, and 2021; marked-to-market liabilities were $1,640 and $1,499 at year-end 2023 and 2022. The company authorized 1.2 billion common and 20 million preferred shares, with none issued; a table reports common and treasury share balances and changes from 2021 through 2023. In 2023, additional paid-in capital decreased $267 from a noncash purchase of subsidiary shares from noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss and Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary: The page presents 2021–2023 changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss by component: currency translation, investment gains and losses, derivative instruments, and defined benefit pension and postretirement plans, including reclassifications and tax-related notes on pension adjustments, amortization, and cash flow hedge losses. It also describes cash flow hedges using foreign currency forwards for expected sales and purchases through 2031 and commodity swaps and purchase contracts to hedge production inputs through 2028.

Notes a 2022 $50 cash-flow-hedge loss reclassification when forecast transactions became unlikely, insignificant undesignated-derivative results, and expected $39 pretax losses to enter earnings in the next 12 months. Describes derivative credit-risk contingencies, a $16 net liability subject to settlement, and no collateral posted. Defines fair-value hierarchy Levels 1–3, presents recurring fair-value assets and liabilities by level for 2023 and 2022, and explains valuation methods for investments and derivatives.

nodes.title: Hedge Reclassifications and Fair Value Measurements
nodes.summary: Describes cash flow hedge losses reclassified from AOCI, insignificant gains or losses on undesignated derivatives, expected future loss reclassification, and credit-related settlement or collateral provisions (with $16 in net derivative liabilities and no collateral posted). Defines the three fair value hierarchy levels and introduces recurring fair value assets, including money market funds, available-for-sale debt investments, other equity investments, and derivatives.

nodes.title: Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text presents fair-value hierarchy information for liabilities and derivatives at December 31, 2023 and 2022, and valuation methods for money market funds, investments, securities, and foreign-currency and commodity derivatives. It reports nonrecurring Level 3 impairment losses and related fair values for investments, operating-lease equipment, property, plant and equipment, and other assets, describing discounted-cash-flow and aircraft-publication valuation methods and management adjustments. It also compares carrying amounts and fair values of notes receivable and debt (excluding finance leases) for both year-ends, with fair values categorized by hierarchy level.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures
nodes.summary: Reports 2023 and 2022 nonrecurring Level 3 impairment losses and fair values for investments, operating lease equipment, property and equipment, and other assets. Describes valuation methods, including discounted cash flows and third-party aircraft publications, with management review and adjustments for asset-specific conditions. Presents carrying amounts and fair values of notes receivable and debt at December 31, 2023 and 2022, including fair-value hierarchy levels.

nodes.title: Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text reports nonrecurring Level 3 fair-value impairment losses and related asset values/classifications for 2023 and 2022. It describes valuation methods: discounted cash flows for investments, property, plant and equipment, and other assets; third-party aircraft publications for operating lease equipment, with quarterly management review and adjustments for asset-specific characteristics or expected sale price. It also presents carrying and fair values of notes receivable and debt at both year-ends, explains their Level 2 valuation methods, notes that fair values of indemnifications and financing commitments cannot practicably be estimated, and states that several other financial instruments’ carrying values approximate fair value (Level 2, except cash at Level 1).

nodes.title: Note 21 – Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: The company faces pending legal proceedings, claims, investigations, and government inquiries involving products, contracts, employment, and other matters; these may lead to financial penalties or restrictions on government contracting and exports. It expects no material financial impact from current matters but cannot estimate losses beyond recorded amounts. Litigation and inquiries arose from the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX crashes. A 2021 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement’s reporting period has ended, and the DOJ is assessing compliance and whether to seek dismissal, subject to court approval. Embraer disputes the company’s 2020 termination of agreements for proposed joint ventures, including an 80% commercial aircraft stake for $4.2 billion; arbitration is expected to resolve in 2024.

nodes.title: Note 22 – Segment and Revenue Information
nodes.summary: Note 22 explains 2023 segment realignment and reclassified interest and debt expense, identifies BCA, BDS, BGS and unallocated activities, and describes each segment’s business and revenue-recognition practices. It reports consolidated and segment revenues by customer geography, contract type and recognition method for 2021–2023, including U.S. government exposure and foreign operating assets. It also gives equity-method earnings and year-end backlog, expected conversion through 2024 and 2027, and uncertainty tied to aircraft deliveries and entry into service.

nodes.title: BGS Revenue, Equity Earnings, and Backlog
nodes.summary: The page presents BGS revenue by year (2021–2023), including commercial and government customer revenue, intersegment eliminations, total revenue, and percentages recognized at a point in time, on fixed-price contracts, and from the U.S. government; the latter includes foreign military sales. It reports equity-method investment income of $70 million in 2023, $56 million in 2022, and $40 million in 2021, with primary drivers varying by segment. It defines backlog, explains revenue conversion, reports $520.195 billion at year-end 2023, estimates conversion of 16% through 2024 and 62% through 2027, and notes uncertainty tied to aircraft deliveries and service-entry timing.

nodes.title: Unallocated Items and Benefit Expenses
key_items: Pension and Other Postretirement Benefit Expense
nodes.summary: Explains that unallocated items include shared services, intersegment sales eliminations, and costs generally assigned under U.S. Government Cost Accounting Standards (CAS), with a table of expense/income components for 2021–2023. Describes CAS allocation of pension and postretirement costs, the difference between GAAP service costs and CAS-allocated costs, and non-operating benefit expenses included in other income; a table gives pension, postretirement, and total FAS/CAS service cost adjustments for 2021–2023.

nodes.title: Segment Assets and Capital Spending
nodes.summary: Reports segment assets at December 31, 2023 and 2022, noting that unallocated assets mainly include cash, investments, tax assets, capitalized interest, centrally managed assets, and intercompany eliminations. Lists capital expenditures by segment and in total for 2021–2023, with unallocated spending mainly for centrally managed assets. Provides depreciation and amortization by segment and centrally managed assets for 2021–2023, explaining that centrally managed costs are allocated to segments by usage and occupancy and detailing the allocations.

nodes.title: Note 23 – Subsequent Events
nodes.summary: After a January 5, 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 door-plug detachment and emergency landing, the FAA grounded and required inspections of affected aircraft, most of the roughly 220 in-service 737-9s. The FAA approved an enhanced inspection process on January 24; operators are returning inspected aircraft to service, and new aircraft will be inspected before delivery. The FAA also opened a Boeing quality-control investigation and said it would not approve 737 MAX production increases or new lines until compliance is established. Boeing cannot yet estimate the financial impact.

nodes.title: Cost Estimates for Fixed-Price Development Contracts - Refer to Notes 1 and 13 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: {"summary":"The critical audit matter concerns estimating costs and margins at completion for long-term fixed-price development contracts, with revenue recognized over time using costs incurred as a measure of progress. Uncertain completion costs, technical and operational complexity, limited historical data, and supply-chain and labor disruptions create risks of reduced margins or reach-forward losses. The auditor applied extensive, specialized procedures to the KC-46A, Commercial Crew, VC-25B, T-7A, and MQ-25 contracts, assessing estimation methods, assumptions, outcomes and estimate-change timing; interviewing project personnel; observing work sites; testing data and controls; developing independent expectations; and comparing past estimates with actual results.

Deloitte evaluated estimation methods and changes, certification milestones and project status, regulator communications, and related controls and data. Deloitte also reports an unqualified opinion that Boeing maintained effective internal control over financial reporting at December 31, 2023, explaining the audit basis, management and auditor responsibilities, and the purpose and limitations of such controls. Deloitte signed in Chicago on January 31, 2024, and noted it has served as auditor since at least 1934.

nodes.title: Boeing Internal Control Audit Opinion

The report explains management’s responsibility, the auditor’s PCAOB registration and independence, and the audit’s reasonable-assurance basis, procedures, and conclusion that it supports the opinion.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Defines internal control over financial reporting as a process providing reasonable assurance of reliable, GAAP-compliant external financial statements. Its policies and procedures support accurate records of transactions and asset dispositions, authorized recording and execution of transactions, and prevention or timely detection of unauthorized asset use or disposition that could materially affect statements. Controls may not prevent or detect all misstatements, and effectiveness may decline in future periods due to changing conditions or reduced compliance. Signed by Deloitte & Touche LLP in Chicago on January 31, 2024.

summary: The auditor gives unqualified opinions that Boeing’s 2021–2023 financial statements comply with U.S. GAAP and that internal controls were effective at December 31, 2023 under COSO’s 2013 framework. nodes.title: SECTION 1. PURPOSE OF THE PLAN
nodes.summary: The Boeing SERP, originally effective in 1999, supplemented Pension Value Plan benefits through Supplemental and Excess Benefit components, merged into one SERP Benefit in 2008 without intended substantive impact. It aims to avoid duplicate nonqualified-plan benefits, with the Committee deciding necessary adjustments. Restatements addressed 409A compliance and clarification; partner and same-sex-spouse survivor benefits were introduced in 2013, discontinued for events after January 1, 2017, and Designated Domestic Partner benefits restored prospectively for events on or after June 1, 2021. Benefit accruals ceased December 31, 2015, except for required Pension Value Plan interest credits.

nodes.title: SECTION 2. DEFINITIONS
nodes.summary: Defines key terms for Boeing’s Supplemental Executive Retirement Plan, generally incorporating Pension Value Plan meanings. It specifies actuarial assumptions for lump sums and spouse/partner options; covered affiliates, employees, service, compensation, benefit commencement, payroll, and company entities; formulas and exclusions for final average pay and incentive pay, including special treatment of absences, reduced service, ULA/USA transfers, and clawbacks; heritage participant, frozen, offset, target, and plan-benefit terms; separation-from-service and specified-employee rules; SERP benefit eligibility and reductions by hire date and vesting; and benefit-accrual freezes effective December 31, 2015, with specified interest-credit exceptions.

nodes.title: SECTION 3. THE SERP BENEFIT
SECTION 3. THE SERP BENEFIT (intro)
nodes.summary: The SERP Benefit is generally the greater of a participant’s vested Supplemental Benefit or vested Excess Benefit, adjusted for commencement before age 65. Participants hired or rehired on or after January 1, 2008 cannot accrue post-date Supplemental Benefits, with specified exceptions to the definition of rehire. Sections 4 and 5 describe the components; shared rules appear in Section 3. From 2008, the components were restated as one benefit without changing the total earned by December 31, 2007. Benefits cannot duplicate individual agreements for participants transferred to ULA or USA. Accrual ceased December 31, 2015, except for PVP Interest Credits.

nodes.title: Special Early Retirement and MDC 50/30 Rules
key_items: A. Special Bridging Rules for Early Retirement Benefits
B. Special Calculation for MDC 50/30 Date After Separation
nodes.summary: For participants separated in a way that allows further vesting credit, special bridging rules apply if, at separation, they are age 54+ with 9+ vesting years (but not yet 55 and 10), or have a Heritage MDC Benefit and are age 54+ with 29+ accumulated service years (but no MDC 50/30 Date). SERP benefits are calculated at the PVP Early Retirement Date, reduced under applicable SERP rules and further adjusted for early commencement using PVP lump-sum factors; Section 6.A.2 timing applies. Participants with a Heritage MDC Benefit, age 49–53, and 29+ service years but no MDC 50/30 Date retain Section 6.A.2 payment timing and receive, at their Early Retirement Date, a lump sum for missed monthly payments from the month after the MDC 50/30 Date to just before that date, with PVP lump-sum interest.

nodes.title: C. Forfeiture
nodes.summary: The Committee may, in its sole discretion, forfeit all or part of a participant’s vested or unvested SERP benefit for specified misconduct during employment or within five years after termination: conviction of certain felonies against the Company or its interests; competition with or adverse activity toward Company business; unauthorized inducement of Company personnel or contractors to leave or breach contracts; or disparaging statements, except legally protected agency statements and sworn testimony. The third and fourth grounds apply only to benefits accrued from January 1, 2008. For benefits already being paid, the Committee may seek legal or equitable recovery. A court ruling limits unenforceable provisions to the broadest enforceable scope. The Committee will also require reimbursement, where appropriate, of SERP benefits tied to incentive awards recovered under the Incentive Compensation Plan’s Clawback Policy.

nodes.title: D. Participants Rehired After Commencement Date
nodes.summary: The section governs SERP benefits when participants are rehired or return after a commencement date, including returns from authorized leave, reduced services, or layoff. Pre-return accruals (“Old SERP Benefit”) continue in their elected payment form. Post-return benefits depend on eligibility and dates: most rehires on or after January 1, 2008 accrue only an Excess Benefit; specified pre-2008 hires returning from leave, reduced service, or layoff may accrue Supplemental and Excess Benefits, recalculated as though no separation occurred and offset for prior benefits and payments. It details calculation, actuarial adjustments, early-retirement reductions, payment timing and form elections, protections for the Old Benefit, and the separate recalculation rules for participants whose subsequent commencement preceded 2008.

nodes.title: E. Participants Rehired Before Commencement Date
nodes.summary: For participants rehired before their SERP commencement date, the text sets rules for separating benefits from prior and post-rehire employment. The Old SERP Benefit is the greater of the vested Supplemental Benefit or vested Excess Benefit from prior service, calculated using age-55 values, applicable early-retirement reductions, and the PVP offset; it is paid under separation-from-service timing rules starting the month after age 55, with payment form elected at commencement. Generally, rehires on or after January 1, 2008 accrue only a post-rehire Excess Benefit, excluding prior service and compensation. Exceptions for certain pre-2008 hires and authorized absences, reduced-service periods, or layoffs allow benefit recalculation as if no separation occurred, subtracting the Old SERP Benefit; post-2008 hires in these cases receive no Supplemental Benefit, and prior nonqualified payments may be offset. New benefits follow continuous-service timing and allow a payment-form election.

nodes.title: F. Pilot Early Leave
nodes.summary: Participants receiving benefits after a deemed separation due to Pilot Early Leave have their benefits recalculated each January 1, starting after benefits commence, under Section 3.D.2.(b) as if no separation occurred. The calculation applies early-retirement reductions and offsets prior payments to determine any additional accruals earned during the prior year. Additional amounts are paid from February 1 in the participant’s originally elected form. Recalculations cannot reduce benefits and stop after the Plan Year following the end of Pilot Early Leave.

Defines the SERP Benefit as the greater of vested Supplemental or Excess Benefits, with age-65 adjustments, accrual limits and cessation, historical restatement rules, and restrictions on duplicating individual agreements. Covers special early-retirement and MDC 50/30 bridging rules; discretionary forfeiture for specified misconduct and reimbursement of clawed-back incentive-related benefits; and benefit calculations, offsets, timing, payment forms, and protections for participants rehired before or after commencement, including exceptions for pre-2008 hires and authorized absences. Also describes annual Pilot Early Leave recalculations and limits.

nodes.title: SECTION 4. THE SUPPLEMENTAL BENEFIT
A. Eligibility and Participation
nodes.summary: Employees qualify for the Supplemental Benefit if they were on the E-Series Payroll on or after January 1, 1999, or met specified 1998 plan-participant and employment-status conditions. Employees who retired January 1, 1999 are excluded. Participation begins when both eligibility and active PVP participation requirements are met; rehires must meet them again. For participants still employed but removed from the E-Series Payroll, the Target Benefit freezes as of the later of January 1, 1999 or removal. Benefit accrual ended December 31, 2015.

nodes.title: B. Amount of Supplemental Benefit
nodes.summary: At normal retirement, the monthly Supplemental Benefit is the greater of the Target Benefit (1.6% times Benefit Service times Total Average Compensation) or, if applicable, the Frozen Benefit, capped at Compensation at Termination divided by 12, minus the PVP Offset Benefit adjusted to a single-life annuity at commencement; the result cannot be below zero. For late retirement, Target Benefit includes compensation and service before and after normal retirement, and the offset reflects late retirement under PVP rules. Accruals ended December 31, 2015.

nodes.title: C. Early Retirement Benefits and Vested Terminated Retirement Benefits
nodes.summary: Subject to Section 6 timing rules and actuarial reductions, participants may begin benefits before Normal Retirement Date under PVP provisions; no unreduced benefit is available, including for Heritage MDC participants age 50 with 30 years of Accumulated Benefit Service. Active employees retiring early have their Target Benefit reduced ¼% per month before age 62, with the Offset Benefit adjusted under the PVP. Vested participants who terminate employment and start benefits early have their Target Benefit reduced ½% per month before age 65, with the Offset Benefit adjusted under the PVP.

nodes.title: D. Disability Retirement Benefits
nodes.summary: Participants on approved medical leave by April 1, 2003, who met PVP disability retirement eligibility by December 1, 2004, were entitled to an unreduced Supplemental Benefit under PVP disability rules. Plan disability benefits were payable only to the extent the participant received PVP disability benefits. This provision applies only to benefits accrued and begun before December 31, 2004, and has no effect thereafter.

nodes.title: E. Vesting
nodes.summary: Supplemental Benefits are payable only when fully vested, generally at the later of full PVP vesting or 36 consecutive months on the E-Series Payroll. Authorized absences count, but non-authorized breaks reset the 36-month period. Specified uninterrupted executive service at ULA or USA counts when directly transferring between qualifying Company and executive roles, subject to limits based on executive status. Certain legacy participants, participants with PVP vesting who die before benefits commence with a surviving spouse, and those eligible for disability retirement receive full vesting. Unvested benefits are generally forfeited upon retirement or separation, except benefits vested during a qualifying deemed separation remain subject to payment-timing rules. After separation following vesting, benefits accrued after rehire or return from authorized absence are fully vested.

nodes.title: F. Transfers
nodes.summary: The section describes transfers into the PVP and this Plan in 1999 and 2000, stating that protections are intended to prevent lost or duplicated benefits. For Heritage Boeing and Heritage MDC participants, it sets special minimum calculations for Final Average Pay and Final Average Incentive Pay based on legacy plans through January 1, 1999; Boeing participants retiring in February or March 1999 may include 1999 incentive awards. It defines Frozen Benefits for Heritage Boeing participants and eligible E-Series employees transferred from the Boeing North American plans. It also excludes the Jeppesen/ASAC Indexing Benefit from the Plan’s Offset Benefit calculation.

The section establishes eligibility, participation, freezes, and the end of benefit accrual in 2015; explains benefit amounts at normal and late retirement, including caps, PVP offsets, and early-retirement reductions; and covers limited historical disability benefits. It sets vesting rules, service and absence treatment, exceptions, forfeitures, and post-rehire protections. It also addresses 1999–2000 transfers, legacy-plan minimum compensation calculations, Frozen Benefits, and exclusion of the Jeppesen/ASAC Indexing Benefit from the offset.

nodes.title: SECTION 5. THE EXCESS BENEFITS
key_items: A. Eligibility; B. Amount of Excess Benefits
C. Adjustments for Commencement Dates other than the Normal Retirement Date
nodes.summary: Employees qualify for an Excess Benefit when a PVP benefit is limited by Code sections 415 or 401(a)(17). The benefit generally equals the PVP benefit calculated without those limits, minus the payable PVP benefit, with a specified additional accrued benefit and compensation-based indexing for Heritage BNA Participants; it must not duplicate benefits under other nonqualified plans. Accruals ceased after December 31, 2015, except required Interest Credits. Non-normal commencement dates and vesting or forfeiture follow PVP rules, with a special calculation for certain late commencements after age 70½.

nodes.title: SECTION 6. PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
key_items: C. Delays in Payment; D. Involuntary Inclusion in Income
nodes.summary: The section sets out SERP benefit payment forms, timing, death benefits, delays, and tax-related distributions. Participants generally receive a single-life annuity but may elect qualifying spouse or, during specified periods, domestic-partner survivor options before commencement; elections then become irrevocable. Defaults depend on marital status, survivor payments may increase if the beneficiary dies first, and benefits worth $15,000 or less are cashed out subject to 409A aggregation rules. Payments generally begin after age 55 and separation, with exceptions for certain Heritage MDC and over-70½ participants; specified employees face a six-month delay, waived on death. Pre-commencement death benefits go to eligible spouses or, in specified periods, domestic partners, with option levels and reductions depending on age and eligibility; some deaths have no payable benefit. Post-commencement benefits follow the elected form, with no payments to a survivor’s estate. Payments may be delayed under 409A, and amounts found currently taxable under 409A are distributed immediately.

nodes.title: SECTION 7. NONASSIGNABILITY
nodes.summary: The SERP benefit generally cannot be assigned, transferred or seized; violations may result in forfeiture. The Committee may recognize qualifying domestic relations orders only if alternate-payee payments start with the Participant’s, and transferred benefits reduce the Participant’s entitlement. Benefits may also be reduced for taxes paid on a Participant’s or surviving spouse’s behalf. The Plan is unfunded, though the Company may use creditor-exposed trusts; participants have only unsecured creditor claims. The Committee administers the Plan and makes binding decisions. The Board may amend or terminate it, subject to protections for payments, survivor rights and eligible employees’ accrued benefits, calculated under Sections 3–5 using specified values as of the change date. Termination generally does not accelerate payment, though a compliant lump sum may be paid. For ERISA purposes, the Plan comprises three distinct plans covering the Supplemental Benefit and Excess Benefits disregarding Code Sections 415 and 401(a)(17). Section 12, Employment Rights, is introduced but contains no text here.

nodes.title: Plan Funding, Administration, Amendments, and Status
nodes.summary: The text notes limits on recognizing domestic relations orders and possible benefit reductions for Company-paid taxes. The Plan is unfunded: no assets are earmarked, and any trusts remain subject to general creditors. A Committee administers the Plan with binding discretionary authority. The Board may amend or terminate it, subject to protections for benefits in payment, joint annuitant rights, and eligible employees’ accrued benefits; distributions generally follow Section 6, though a lump sum may be allowed under Code section 409A. For ERISA purposes, the Plan comprises three distinct plans covering the Supplemental Benefit and Excess Benefits disregarding Code sections 415 and 401(a)(17).

nodes.title: SECTION 12. EMPLOYMENT RIGHTS
nodes.summary: The Plan creates no employment rights and does not limit the Company’s ability to terminate employment, with or without cause. Claims and denial reviews follow the PVP procedures. Plan terms should be construed to avoid taxation under Code Section 409A. Federal law governs validity and construction, supplemented where permissible by Illinois law; invalid provisions do not affect the remainder. Court actions for benefits must be brought within 180 days after an appeal decision or, if no appeal is filed, after the appeal deadline.

nodes.title: Plan Claims, Compliance, and Legal Provisions
nodes.summary: The Plan does not guarantee continued employment or limit the Company’s right to terminate employment. Benefit claims and appeals follow PVP procedures. Plan terms are intended to avoid taxation under Code Section 409A. Federal law and, where permissible, Illinois law govern; invalid provisions do not affect the remainder. Court actions over benefit claims must be filed within 180 days after an appeal decision or, absent an appeal, within 180 days after the appeal deadline.

Clawback Policy Applicable to Covered Compensation
Clawback Policy Applicable to Incentive-Based Compensation Generally; Administration and Interpretation; Disclosure
Clawback Policy Applicable to Incentive-Based Compensation Generally
summary: Boeing’s June 27, 2023 policy establishes recovery of erroneously awarded compensation after accounting restatements, as required by SEC/NYSE rules, and discretionary recovery of incentive compensation for fraud, bribery, related failures to report, or safety-compromising misconduct or negligence. It specifies limited, documented exceptions; bars insurance, reimbursement, or indemnification for required recovery; assigns administration, amendment, offset, and disclosure authority; and defines key terms, eligibility, calculation, recovery periods, and triggering dates.
